First question--How does a case get assigned to a Judge? answer--This depends on the jurisdiction you are located in. The first issue that needs to be addressed is, which Court is the case in? In the US, there are Federal Courts that cover the entire country, and State Courts that cover every individual state. There are also Municipal Courts for most incorporated cities and towns. The type of case determines which Court is proper. There is overlap between the jurisdictions, meaning that certain matters, but not all, could be heard either by the Federal or State Court, or by either State or Municipal Court. I'm not aware of any type of matter that could be heard in any one of the three, but I suppose it's certainly possible. In criminal cases, Federal Courts hear criminal charges under federal law, state courts hear criminal charges under state law, and muni courts hear "criminal" (although usually decriminalized) charges under local city ordinances. There is significant overlap between the state, federal, and local laws, so the law enforcement office bringing the charges usually has a choice of which Court to file the charges in, and it's usually determined by that office's policy although it could be done for strategic reasons. Usually there's no bar to bringing the same charges in each court at the same time, either. If you're a criminal defendant you don't have much choice in where your case will be heard. For civil cases, I don't know of any muni courts that hear civil disputes, except for quasi-criminal charges like parking tickets and traffic offenses that might be considered civil if they're only seeking fines. State and Federal Courts have significant overlap in jurisdiction in civil cases, so many cases (but not all) can be brought in either State or Federal Court. In cases of "concurrent jurisdiction" the Plaintiff is the "master of his case" and gets to decide where to file. There is a process to remove a case from state court to federal court if certain requirements are met, even if it could be heard by the state court. There is also a process for remand back to state court. Once you determine the right court system to file the case in, there is also an issue of which venue to file it in. Most state courts are set up with a different court-district for each county, or sometimes multiple counties or some other way. Each state will have different rules about which county court you can bring the case in, but it will based on the location of the parties and the subject matter of the controversy. Federal Courts are also divided into different districts, but there's fewer federal district courts so some are for entire states and other states are divided into different federal district courts. Again, the proper venue is determined by the location of the parties and the subject matter at issue. It's entirely possible, and maybe even likely, that multiple venues are appropriate. Again, Plaintiff gets to decide where to file, but there's a process to change the venue if Defendants object, although Defendants will have to show that the venue selected is improper, not just that they'd prefer a different venue. Once the proper venue is established, it's up to that district to assign it an actual individual judge. Some state court districts might only have a single judge, which means he's the one you get. All federal districts and most state court districts will have several presiding judges though. The decision to assign the case to a specific judge is usually (always in fed court, but not sure about all state courts) up to the "chief judge" in that district, who will usually have a "random" process for assigning cases.

Second question--Is there a process to get a new judge once one has been assigned? Yes. Even if you're in a county with only one judge, there still has to be a process, because of exactly the reason you mentioned, potential conflicts of interest. Some jurisdictions even allow you to "spin the wheel" and be randomly assigned to a new judge just by requesting it. You will almost always have to pay a fee for this, and usually it can only be done once, and must be done before any rulings in the case have been made. As was discussed above, Plaintiff has significant control over the case and how it's filed, and so even if your jurisdiction doesn't allow peremptory challenges of judges, you may have the option, depending on timing issues, to voluntarily dismiss, without prejudice, and refile it, and get randomly reassigned again. This only works if you are within the statute of limitations to refile the case. If those options aren't available, getting the case to a different judge can be a lot more complicated. If the Judge believes he or she has a conflict of interest though, they are actually required to recuse themselves and have it assigned to a different judge. Even if you're in a one-judge county, the matter can be heard by a judge from another county if the only judge recuses. The judge also has a duty to recuse not just in situations where they actually have a conflict of interest, but also in situations where there could be the appearance of a conflict of interest. So this is pretty broad. Even if the Judge doesn't voluntarily recuse right away, gently raising the issue at the first hearing can be enough to get them to voluntarily recuse, again, because the mere appearance of a conflict is sufficient. Judges don't usually want to preside over cases that could get them accused of being biased. If the judge still refuses to recuse, there is definitely a process to file a motion to disqualify the judge, which will likely be heard by the chief judge who will make the decision. The rules may vary slightly but you will have to demonstrate the existence of a conflict, and possibly also have to show a decision that was made that shows some bias against you. The judge will have a chance to respond to the motion and explain that they are not biased. Motions to disqualify will almost never be granted. The Judge will often recuse in response, but if they oppose it, in my experience, it's rare that the chief judge will grant a motion over the objection of the judge who claims to be unbiased and able to decide fairly and impartially. Basically, the judge accused of the conflict is usually smart enough to figure out if it will be granted, and if it will, they just recuse. Merely making rulings against you in the past is insufficient to show bias or a conflict of interest. Financial interest related to the outcome of the case will almost always be sufficient. Family relationships can implicate conflicts, but they have to be close relationships, the closer, the more likely there is a conflict. A judge shouldn't ever hear cases where immediate family is a party or attorney, but cousins, especially more distant than a first cousin, is a real grey area, it just depends on the relationship. Friends are even more difficult, because Judges have a lot of friends usually, and friendships are very difficult to prove.

If you want to provide more details about the Court, type of case, and nature of the conflict I can provide additional information. You should not consider anything I've said or will say to be legal advice, however.

It sucks, but you usually can't do anything with the lower level judges.* Essentially, showing a conflict of interest isn't enough. You need show there was a conflict, and that the conflict caused an adverse outcome. Note that you must show the adverse outcome was due to the conflict - just because the judge is conflicted doesn't mean the judge was wrong.

The two main ways of appealing a conflict of interest are appeals, and interlocutory appeals (very hard to do). An interlocutory appeal is an appeal during a proceeding (that is, final judgment hasn't been rendered yet). So for example, you make a motion on X, the judge rules against you, you appeal the ruling on the motion and try to prove it was due to the conflict of interest. Again, very, very hard to do, as judges have wide discretion. (And even then, you might only get the motion reversed, but the case would likely continue with the same judge).

Simply working through the process, receiving a final judgment, and then appealing that has a much better chance of success. You do a full appeal, and one of the arguments you make in your appeal is the judge's conflict of interest directly affecting the outcome of the case (and of course, you lay out your evidence for it).

*In most places in America. Note that every state, county, and town have different rules and different procedures. You should check with a local attorney licensed in your area to understand the laws that apply to your situation. This post is not legal advice.
